Table of Contents
1	PURPOSE AND MS QUALIFICATION LENS	3
2	CUSTOMER DISCUSSION TRIGGERS AND EY CONVERSION MOVES	4
3	RECOMMENDED EY CONVERSATION TECHNIQUE	9
4	WHEN NOT TO FORCE AN MS CONSTRUCT	9
5	SUGGESTED POSITIONING STATEMENT	9



 
1	Purpose and MS Qualification Lens

Purpose of this document is to help EY teams recognize customer statements that may indicate a Managed Services opportunity and convert them into a structured, value-led conversation. 
Use the following three tests before positioning Managed Services:
•	Run / Operate Scope: The activity is recurring and can be operated, not merely a one-off advisory or implementation task.
•	Measurable Service Delivery: Outputs and performance can be governed through KPIs, SLAs, controls and clear accountability.
•	Transition Feasibility: Scope, knowledge, access, governance and operating responsibilities can be transitioned responsibly

2	Customer Discussion Triggers and EY Conversion Moves

Customer statement	What it may indicate	EY MS conversation move	Value to position	Discovery question
“Our team spends most of its time on BAU and firefighting.”	Recurring operations are consuming strategic capacity.	Offer an EY-operated BAU service with defined scope, SLAs, governance, automation and continuous improvement.	Release retained capacity; improve discipline and predictability.	Which recurring activities consume the most capacity, and what strategic work is being delayed?
“We need to reduce operating cost this year.”	Immediate efficiency or productivity mandate.	Baseline demand, effort, process variation, automation potential, location mix and unit cost; shape a productivity-led MS construct.	Predictable cost, productivity improvement and benefits transparency.	Is the priority cost alone, or must service quality, controls and experience also improve?
“We cannot hire or retain the required skills.”	Specialist capability gap or unstable capacity.	Provide access to a scalable pool of domain, technology and operational specialists rather than client-by-client hiring.	Access to scarce skills, continuity and lower key-person dependency.	Which skills create delivery bottlenecks, and are the needs recurring or seasonal?
“A few critical people hold all the knowledge.”	Concentration and business-continuity risk.	Position knowledge transition, SOPs, knowledge management, cross-skilling and succession coverage.	Institutionalized knowledge and stronger resilience.	What would happen if those individuals were unavailable during a critical period?
“Volumes fluctuate during month-end, year-end or peak seasons.”	Demand variability makes fixed capacity inefficient.	Explore scalable capacity or transaction pricing with volume bands and surge mechanisms.	Flexible capacity and reduced idle-cost exposure.	What are the normal, peak and exceptional volumes, and how much advance visibility is available?
“Turnaround time is inconsistent and the backlog keeps increasing.”	Capacity, workflow or governance issue.	Offer an output-led service governed by backlog, ageing and turnaround SLAs, supported by standardization and automation.	Faster processing and clearer accountability.	What are the current backlog, ageing profile, required TAT and main delay drivers?
“Service quality varies by location, team or vendor.”	Fragmented processes and inconsistent controls.	Standardise SOPs, QA controls, training, service levels and central governance.	Consistent quality, fewer errors and improved visibility.	Where is variation highest, and is quality measured consistently?
“We receive too many complaints or escalations.”	Weak service experience or issue resolution.	Shape an experience-led MS model with omnichannel intake, case management, knowledge-enabled resolution and experience KPIs.	Faster resolution and fewer repeat contacts.	What are the top complaint categories, repeat-contact rates and escalation drivers?
“We meet the SLA, but the business is still unhappy.”	Metrics measure activity rather than business value.	Redesign scorecards around experience, effectiveness, availability and first-time-right—not response time alone.	Align service performance with business expectations.	Which business outcomes or user experiences are missing from the current SLA framework?
“We have multiple vendors, but no one owns the end-to-end outcome.”	Fragmented accountability and hand-offs.	Discuss service integration, end-to-end process ownership, integrated reporting and cross-vendor governance.	Clear ownership and faster resolution of cross-vendor issues.	Where do issues move between providers without a clear owner?
“We are paying several vendors and do not know whether we get value.”	Poor spend visibility and supplier fragmentation.	Offer service baselining, supplier rationalization, should-cost analysis and performance governance.	Cost transparency, reduced overlap and stronger accountability.	Can spend, scope, performance and contractual commitments be linked by supplier?
“Our reporting is manual and leadership lacks a reliable view.”	Fragmented data and limited operational visibility.	Position an MS control tower with automated dashboards, demand/SLA reporting, root-cause analysis and benefits tracking.	Trusted management information and proactive decisions.	Which decisions are delayed because data is unavailable or manually consolidated?
“We repeatedly face the same incidents or errors.”	Reactive operations without problem management.	Shift from ticket closure to RCA, permanent fixes, knowledge reuse and automation.	Lower repeat demand and improved stability.	What proportion of demand is repeatable, and how are permanent fixes prioritized?
“Our application team only has time to keep the lights on.”	Technical debt and innovation backlog.	Propose run-and-transform AMS covering operations, engineering, backlog reduction, automation and modernization.	Stability plus capacity for innovation.	How much capacity is spent on incidents versus enhancements and modernization?
“The new system is live, but we are struggling to stabilise it.”	Need for post-transformation operations.	Extend the programme into stabilization, application support, adoption, optimization and backlog management.	Protect transformation investment and accelerate benefits.	Who owns the platform after hypercare, and how will optimization be governed?
“We bought tools, but adoption and utilisation remain low.”	Technology investment is not producing value.	Offer platform operations covering adoption, administration, optimization, release management and value tracking.	Improved return on investment and feature adoption.	Which capabilities are underused, and how are realized benefits measured?
“Automation and AI pilots are not scaling into BAU.”	Innovation lacks operational ownership.	Offer AI-enabled operations with use-case intake, controlled deployment, human oversight, measurement and refinement.	Sustainable productivity and institutionalized innovation.	Who owns each use case after pilot, and how are accuracy, controls and benefits monitored?
“Our processes depend on spreadsheets and emails.”	Manual, fragmented and weakly controlled workflows.	Propose process discovery followed by workflow-enabled operations, automation and exception management.	Traceability, shorter turnaround and fewer errors.	Which activities are rules-based, repetitive and most prone to rework?
“Audit observations keep recurring.”	Controls are not embedded in BAU.	Position a control-enabled MS model with evidence management, exception monitoring and remediation tracking.	Audit readiness and reduced repeat findings.	Which findings recur, who owns remediation, and how is evidence managed?
“Regulatory requirements change too quickly for our team.”	Need for sustained specialist capability.	Explore domain-led operations combining monitoring, impact assessment, execution, controls and reporting, within applicable responsibility boundaries.	Specialist access, consistent execution and compliance visibility.	Which activities are recurring, and which decisions must remain with management?
“Security alerts are increasing and we cannot investigate everything.”	High-volume monitoring and capacity constraint.	Discuss managed monitoring, triage, escalation, threat intelligence and incident workflow.	Improved coverage and consistent response.	What is the alert volume, investigation backlog and critical-system profile?
“Cloud cost is increasing, but we cannot explain why.”	Weak consumption governance and optimization.	Position continuous FinOps operations covering attribution, tagging, optimization, forecasting and governance.	Cost transparency and continuous optimization.	Can consumption be attributed to business owners, products and environments?
“Applications or infrastructure experience frequent downtime.”	Reactive maintenance or weak observability.	Offer observability, incident/problem management, capacity management and reliability improvement against business-service KPIs.	Improved resilience and faster recovery.	Which services create the greatest business impact when unavailable?
“Our data is inconsistent and takes too long to reconcile.”	Recurring data-quality and operational problem.	Shape managed data operations covering ingestion monitoring, quality rules, reconciliation, exceptions and stewardship support.	Trusted data and less manual reconciliation.	Where do data breaks occur, and which decisions or reports are affected?
“Finance spends too much time on reconciliations and close.”	Transactional effort and manual close activities.	Position managed finance operations covering processing, reconciliation, reporting, controls and optimization.	Faster close, reduced effort and improved control.	Which close activities are most labour-intensive, late or error-prone?
“HR receives the same employee queries repeatedly.”	High-volume repeatable service demand.	Offer employee service operations using tiered support, knowledge, self-service, workflow and AI-enabled handling.	Faster and more consistent employee support.	What proportion of requests are repetitive versus requiring specialist judgement?
“We need 24×7 support, but an internal model is too expensive.”	Coverage requirement exceeds current economics.	Explore a shared/global model with follow-the-sun coverage, severity SLAs, on-call arrangements and escalation.	Broader coverage and predictable service.	Which services genuinely require 24×7 coverage and what recovery targets are critical?
“We are entering new markets and cannot build operations fast enough.”	Need for rapid, repeatable scaling.	Position modular operations with standard processes, scalable capacity and local compliance support where appropriate.	Faster mobilisation and lower set-up burden.	Which capabilities must be live first, and what country and volume requirements apply?
“We are considering a GCC but are unsure how to build and operate it.”	Operating-model, talent and mobilisation challenge.	Discuss build-operate-transfer, managed GCC or capability-centre constructs across transition, talent, process, governance and technology.	Faster capability creation and controlled transition.	Is the priority speed, long-term ownership, cost optimization or a combination?
“The business expects more without additional resources.”	Demand-capacity imbalance.	Offer demand management, service catalogue, automation and tiered delivery through a scalable MS construct.	Demand control, scalable capacity and transparent prioritization.	Which requests are recurring, and how are they prioritized against capacity?
“We need predictable costs rather than continuous change requests.”	Need for commercial certainty and clear boundaries.	Explore fixed-fee, subscription, capacity-band or unit pricing with baselines, volume assumptions and change mechanisms.	Budget predictability and commercial transparency.	How stable are scope and volumes, and what demand drivers could change cost?
“We need a partner to continuously improve—not just provide resources.”	Direct opening for mature Managed Services.	Shape an outcome-led service with productivity commitments, automation pipeline and innovation governance.	Continuous value improvement rather than staff augmentation.	Which improvement outcomes should the provider own, and how will they be measured?


3	Recommended EY Conversation Technique

1. Acknowledge the pain	Reflect the client’s operational challenge in business language.
2. Quantify the impact	Establish volumes, backlog, cost, errors, downtime, complaints, risk exposure and internal effort. Avoid unsupported savings claims.
3. Test MS suitability	Confirm the scope is recurring, measurable, transitionable and governable.
4. Reframe resources to results	Move from “How many FTEs?” to “What outputs, service levels, controls and improvements are required?”
5. Shape the value construct	Combine domain expertise, scalable delivery, technology, automation, governance and continuous improvement.
6. Close a practical next step	Agree a diagnostic, discovery workshop, baseline exercise or pilot for one process, service tower or geography.

4	When Not to Force an MS Construct

•	The requirement is purely one-off advisory or implementation work.
•	The client only wants named resources under its direct day-to-day control.
•	There is no recurring service, operational ownership or measurable output.
•	There is no sponsor, transition appetite, governance or funding.
•	The requested construct would transfer responsibilities that must remain with client management.
•	The process baseline, dependencies or data are insufficient to price or accept outcome risk.
5	Suggested Positioning Statement

  01. Managed Service Qualification
Purpose: Identify whether an opportunity is suitable for Managed Services.

Qualification Tests:
• Run / Operate Scope
• Measurable Service Delivery
• Transition Feasibility

Conversation Technique:
1. Acknowledge the pain
2. Quantify impact
3. Test suitability
4. Reframe resources to outcomes
5. Shape value proposition
6. Agree next step

Do not position Managed Services for one-time work, staff augmentation only, non-recurring work, or engagements without measurable outcomes or transition readiness.
02. Conversation Triggers
BAU & firefighting, cost reduction, talent shortage, knowledge concentration, seasonal demand, backlog growth, inconsistent SLAs, multiple vendors, manual reporting, repeat incidents, application support overload, low technology adoption, AI pilots, spreadsheet-based processes, audit findings, regulatory pressure, security monitoring, cloud cost, downtime, data quality, finance reconciliation, HR support, 24x7 support, expansion, GCC, demand vs capacity, predictable pricing, continuous improvement.
03. Discovery Questions
Understand current process, ownership, volumes, SLAs, KPIs, backlog, automation, vendors, governance, risks, business outcomes, sponsors and timeline.

Cloud example:
• Who owns cloud spend?
• Is tagging standardized?
• Are chargebacks implemented?
• How is optimization measured?
• Which workloads drive cost?
04. Positioning Statements
Position EY around outcome-led services, governance, automation, operational excellence, predictable cost, scalability, resilience, customer experience, risk reduction and continuous improvement.
05. Objection Handling
We don't want outsourcing → Governance remains with client.
We already have vendors → Improve end-to-end accountability.
No budget → Start with a pilot.
Security won't allow it → Operate within client controls.
We need our own people → Free internal teams for strategic work.
06. Industry Playbooks
Banking: AML/KYC, fraud, loan ops.
Healthcare: patient services, HIS support, revenue cycle.
Retail: POS, inventory, omnichannel.
Manufacturing: SAP AMS, plant IT.
Energy: field ops, outage management.
Telecom: NOC, customer ops.
Public Sector: citizen services, shared services.
07. Real Client Scenarios
Closing our books takes 12 days.
Finance still works in Excel.
We have 19 vendors managing SAP.
Our backlog keeps increasing.
Nobody trusts the dashboard.
Cloud costs doubled.
HR receives repetitive payroll questions.
Security alerts are overwhelming.
We cannot hire skilled engineers.
Plant downtime is increasing.
08. Managed Services Solution Library
For each solution capture: Name, Problem, Scope, Deliverables, KPIs, SLAs, Automation, Governance, Commercial Model, Transition.
Examples: Finance Ops, HR Ops, AMS, FinOps, Cyber Ops, Data Ops, Contact Center, Procurement, GCC.
09. Meeting Playbooks
Before: Review client and industry.
During: Listen, qualify, position, validate.
After: Summarize, recommend workshop/assessment/pilot.
Assets: Elevator pitch, executive pitch, workshop agenda, follow-up email.
10. Glossary
AMS, BAU, GCC, KPI, SLA, RCA, FinOps, RPA, NOC, TAT, Managed Services, Control Tower.
